title: Shichi-Go-San: Japan's Special Day for Children
paragraphs: Every November, children across Japan dress up in their best clothes and visit shrines and temples with their families. They do this to celebrate Shichi-Go-San, a traditional Japanese event for young children.

Shichi-Go-San means "seven-five-three" in Japanese. The holiday celebrates girls aged three and seven, and boys aged three and five. Families give thanks for their children's growth and pray for their future health.
The traditional date is November 15, but many families now celebrate on any weekend during November.

For Shichi-Go-San, children receive a special candy called chitose ame. This long, thin candy is usually red or white, and its name means "thousand-year candy," representing the hope that children will live long, healthy lives.

The candy comes in colorful paper bags, often with pictures of cranes and turtles, because in Japan, these animals are symbols of long life and good luck. Parents can buy this candy at supermarkets, and some shrines even give it to children as a gift when they visit.
Shichi-Go-San wasn't always a single event, however. It's based on several different celebrations that wealthy Japanese families held in centuries past when their children reached certain ages.

At three, children could traditionally begin growing their hair instead of having it cut very short. At five, boys wore traditional trousers, called hakama, for the first time. And at seven, girls began wearing traditional kimono belts, called obi.
These ages were important because medical care was much more basic in the past, and many children died young. So families wanted to celebrate their children reaching these ages.
Over time, these traditions came together and spread to ordinary families across Japan, and by the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Shichi-Go-San had become a popular celebration.
Today, Shichi-Go-San is still an important family event. Families continue to celebrate their children's growth and wish them a long, healthy life.
